_note: THE ATTRIBUTE-BINDING FOLD. Markup has exactly one way to write a consumer attribute -
`name="…"` - and three things an author can mean by it: a literal, one value, or a
sentence built out of values. The fold is the pure syntactic function that decides which,
and it is the same function on all three renderers because a component that receives an
object on one and the string "[object Object]" on another is not one component.
static  - no `{{` anywhere. The attribute IS its own text.
value   - the trimmed template is exactly ONE `{{ … }}` and nothing else. The
attribute carries the EXPRESSION'S VALUE: an object stays an object, a
number stays a number, null stays null.
text    - anything else (a mix of literal and holes, or several holes). Every hole is
string-coerced and concatenated, because a sentence is a string.
WHY `value` HAD TO EXIST. Before this fold a .dsx component's props were interpolated
unconditionally, so every prop arrived as a string. That is invisible for a label and
fatal for structure: `<Node data="{{ item.children }}"/>` handed the child the text
"[object Object],[object Object]" and a recursive component - a tree rendering itself -
could not pass its own children down, which is the shape every outliner, file browser,
comment thread and DOM inspector is made of. The module-facet path had ALREADY made this
decision correctly and privately (dom/src/mount.ts mountFacet), so the two component
kinds disagreed about what a prop is. This corpus is that decision, promoted to law and
made the same in three places.
SCANNING MATCHES INTERPOLATION, deliberately. A hole ends at the FIRST `}}` - the same
naive scan the interpolator itself performs. A closer inside a string literal therefore
ends the hole on every renderer identically; the fold is never allowed to disagree with
the interpolator about where an expression stops, because a disagreement there is a
silent type change, and a shared wrong answer is repairable while a split one is not.
WHITESPACE IS TRIMMED before the shape is judged, so a hole indented across lines in
real markup is still one hole. Interior whitespace inside the braces belongs to the
expression and the evaluator trims it in turn.
Runners - three implementations, all three execute this file:
TS     - OpenSource/Web/packages/kernel/test/composition-conformance.test.ts (per-PR)
Kotlin - :core CompositionConformanceTest (per-PR, gradle, SDK-free)
Swift  - CompositionConformance, driven by RecordMain.swift on the record lane

fold.name: literal with braces that are not holes
single brace pair is not a hole
sole hole holding a spaced object literal
sole hole holding a spaced array literal
unspaced object literal loses its last brace to the scan
object literal flush against the closer is NOT a sole hole

_foldNote: THE BRACE EDGE, pinned rather than papered over. A hole ends at the first `}}`, so an
object literal written the conventional way - `{{ { id: row.id } }}`, with a space
before the closer - is a perfectly ordinary sole hole and carries the object. The same
literal written flush - `{{ {id: 1}}}` - is not: the object's own `}` plus the hole's
first `}` form the terminator, the hole closes one character early, and the trailing
`}` becomes literal text, so the fold reports `text`.
No renderer is allowed to get clever and brace-balance its way out of this. The fold
must agree with the interpolator about where an expression stops, and the interpolator
scans naively; a renderer that balanced braces here would be the only one that did,
which is a silent type split - strictly worse than a limitation all three share and
an author can see. The fix in markup is a space, which is how anyone writes it anyway.

typed.name: zero survives as a number, not the empty string
false survives as a boolean, not the string "false"
absent reads as null, not the string "null"
a member read off an object prop stays typed
a sentence is a string even when its holes are typed
two typed holes concatenate as strings
a static attribute is its own text
an object in a sentence stringifies, and that is why sole holes exist
a spaced object literal evaluates to an object
a flush object literal falls back to text

_note: THE RECURSION CONTRACT. A component that names itself is the point of the `value`
kind: a tree renders one node and hands the node's own children to a nested instance
of itself. That only terminates because the DATA terminates - the child list runs out.
So the depth cap is NOT a feature budget and must never be tuned to taste. It exists
for exactly one case: data that is corrupt or cyclic, where the child list never runs
out and the renderer would recurse until the stack dies. A crash is the worst possible
answer to bad data, so the cap converts it into a bounded render. Legitimate nesting
must never reach it.
`depth` counts component EXPANSIONS from the surface root, and the cap is uniform
across renderers so a tree that draws on one draws on all three.
